name: Directional Permeability
question: Does the sample conduct flow equally in different directions?
blurb: The same grain pack driven along y instead of x. The permeability tensor of a random pack is nearly isotropic; an arranged or elongated pack is not.
physics:
Soils, rocks, filters, catalyst beds, even bone — all are porous: solid matrices threaded by pore space. When you drive fluid through, it cannot go straight; it winds through the connected pores, speeding up in the throats and stalling in the dead ends. Henry Darcy discovered in 1856, while engineering Dijon's water supply, that despite this complexity the average flow rate is simply proportional to the pressure gradient. The proportionality constant — the permeability k — packs all the pore geometry into one number with units of area.

Permeability is what petroleum engineers need to predict oil recovery, what hydrologists need for groundwater, and what battery and fuel-cell designers tune in porous electrodes. You cannot read k off a photo of the pores; you have to solve the flow. 'Digital rock physics' does exactly that — simulate the pore-scale flow in a 3D/2D image of the material and measure the averaged response. That is precisely what this exhibit does with lattice-Boltzmann.

Here a constant body force drives flow through a random grain pack in a periodic box; once steady, the volume-averaged velocity ⟨u⟩ gives k = ν⟨u⟩/g. Drop the porosity and the tortuous paths choke down — permeability falls steeply, as the Kozeny–Carman relation predicts.
terms:
• ⟨u⟩ — the velocity averaged over the whole sample (Darcy/superficial velocity)
• k — permeability: the area-dimensioned measure of how easily fluid passes
• μ = ρν — dynamic viscosity; ∇p — the driving pressure gradient (here a body force)
• φ — porosity, the void fraction; k climbs steeply with φ
• Kozeny–Carman: k ≈ φ³d²/[180(1−φ)²] links k to porosity and grain size d
numerics: The same D2Q9 lattice-Boltzmann scheme, here in a periodic box driven by a constant body force (Guo forcing) through a random grain pack, in the viscous (Stokes) regime, along x or y. Permeability is k = ν U_D/g with U_D the superficial velocity (flow averaged over the whole sample, solids counting as zero) and g the body force per unit mass; the pore-average velocity U_D/φ is reported separately.
ic: Fluid at rest inside a random grain pack (equilibrium populations at zero velocity), then accelerated by the body force; the permeability is read from the final state.
bc: Periodic in x and y with a constant body force along x or y; no-slip bounce-back on every grain surface.
validation: Numerical check: on a sample of horizontal solid slabs the solver gives k_x ≫ k_y (tests/), so the directional measurement is trustworthy; for a random pack k_x ≈ k_y is expected.

experiment.name: Porous flow
experiment.question: How readily does a grain pack transmit fluid, and why?

compare.text: Similar porosity, different arrangement: both measured porosities are shown; k differs by connectivity.
Same sample driven along x and along y: k_x versus k_y (force magnitude held).

params.name: porosity
params.label: Porosity  φ
params.help: Fraction of the sample that is open pore space. Lower porosity (denser grain packing) → far lower permeability.

params.name: grain
params.label: Grain size
params.help: Radius of the packed grains as a fraction of the sample height.

params.name: seed
params.label: Random seed
params.help: Seed of the random grain arrangement: change it to compare samples with the same porosity but different connectivity.

params.name: direction
params.label: Driving direction
params.help: Direction of the body force. Run both to measure the directional permeability k_x and k_y of the same sample (anisotropy).

params.name: strength
params.label: Driving strength
params.help: Multiplier on the body force (1 = 1.2e-5 lattice units). In the Darcy regime k must not depend on it — sweep it to check linearity.

params.name: resolution
params.label: Resolution
params.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

params.name: duration
params.label: Duration (×)
params.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
